Q: How do I filter by contents of an unnamed object in an array with JSONPath? A:

Answer:

Tony Chu's accepted answer is spot on with the expression $["0"][?@[1].zp.udm=="50"]. I want to expand on the underlying mechanics of why your initial attempts didn't work, as understanding this is key to mastering JSONPath's filter context.

Why Your .* and .. Attempts Failed

The crucial concept here is the "current item" referenced by @ inside a filter expression.

  • When you write a filter like [? ... ], you are iterating over an array.

  • Inside that filter, the @ symbol represents each individual element of that array, one at a time.

In your data, each element of the outermost array is itself an array (e.g., ["Why are we here", {...}]). So, within the filter, @ is this entire inner array. To access its second element (the unnamed object), you must use an explicit index, @[1], because @ itself is an array, not an object. That's precisely what Tony's [?@[1].zp.udm=="50"] does.

Your attempts with @*.zp.udm or @..zp.udm didn't work because:

  • .* is a wildcard for object member values, not array elements.

  • .. is a recursive descent operator.
    Neither is the correct tool to navigate an array by positional index, which is what your data structure requires.

Understanding the Result Wrapping and How to Handle It in Code

A key point that often causes confusion: JSONPath always returns a list of matches, even if there's only one match or zero matches. That's why the evaluator wraps Tony's result in an extra [...].

Here's how to handle this reliably in a real-world application:

JavaScript example:


const query = 'Your JSONPath expression'; // $["0"][?@[1].zp.udm=="50"]
const resultList = jsonpath.query(data, query);

if (resultList.length > 0) {
    const actualMatch = resultList[0];
    console.log(actualMatch); // Your desired array: ["Why are we here", {...}]
} else {
    console.log("No match found");
}

Python example:

import jsonpath_ng

query = '$["0"][?@[1].zp.udm=="50"]'
result_list = jsonpath_ng.parse(query).find(data)

if result_list:
    actual_match = result_list[0].value
    print(actual_match) # Your desired array: ["Why are we here", {...}]
else:
    print("No match found")

Always check if the result list is non-empty before accessing the first element to avoid exceptions in your code.

Summary for Future JSONPath Challenges

When filtering based on fields inside an anonymous object that sits at a known position within an array, always use the explicit index syntax @[index] to first navigate to that object, then continue drilling down.

  • Correct: [?@[1].zp.udm=="50"]

  • Incorrect: [?@*.zp.udm=="50"]

I hope this clarifies the mechanics behind the solution!

Q: SQLAlchemy DateTime timezone A:

If this upgrade is only due to the deprecation warning related to Python3.11+ and you had to replace this datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc)

But timezone aware raise a new set of problems, including receiving from the DB a non-timezone aware ( but value match the TZ you need ) which results the error:

TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes

Then I just simply removed the timezone-aware after generating the correct time I needed, meaning

# UTC time, no TZ aware, but show deprecation warning
deprecated_date = datetime.utcnow()

# UTC time + timezone aware, but during compare it resulted with 
# TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
newway_timezone_aware_date = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

# UTC time, no Python deprecation warning, and not timezone aware.
utc_no_tz_aware = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(tzinfo=None)    # works for me

Q: Choosing between backend or frontend stack A:

If you hate HTML then there's certainly not much mileage in being a front-end web developer. But that doesn't rule out other types of client-side coding such as mobile apps, desktop apps, games etc. Of course you could also go down the backend route but that's certainly not your only option, and it's not a binary choice.

Like many of us, you may just end up doing a bit of everything at different times depending on what's needed. In some organisations the more things you can turn your hand to the more useful you are. In other, possibly larger, places you tend to get more specialisation.

Q: Spring thinks that my post processor doesn't implement the right interface if load time weaving is enabled and I use a factory method to create it A:

Okay, so, it turns out that I omitted a key fact: this is on Java 16+.

Why this matters: Spring tries to use Class.findLoadedClass() on the "normal" to figure out if it should load things using the disposable loader or not. This method is protected so Spring can't get to it... so it tries to use reflection. (See the static init block in ContextTypeMatchClassLoader.)

In Java 15, this would succeed by default, but the JVM would log a warning. In Java 16, this fails by default, but Spring catches the exception, and logs it at "debug" level, as if this is "no big deal". Since it can't figure out which classes the disposable loader should load, it loads "more than it should". And then this breaks everything.

As for why this wasn't breaking in prod? It turns out that there we were already running with

--add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED

so there it works fine. Solution is to just add this to the test.

Alternatively, if you have Spring on the module path, use that instead of ALL-UNNAMED
